# Volume 5 — CHAPTER XXXI. RUPERT DOES PENANCE

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

“I fail to understand why any punishment should be given to us,” Grace remarked, appearing quite cross. “No wrongdoing was committed by us. Our fear was something we were unable to control. Furthermore, father will suffer no injury from it. What happened was merely an accident.”
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0000 }

“You proved to be cowards,” Tobias declared with the contempt of a judge, “and you succumbed to your fear. That is the reason you ought to be disciplined. Everyone is going to mock you over this, and the family is disgraced by it.”
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0001 }

“Were you aware of how terrible everything was,” Grace stated while shivering, “you’d believe our punishment was already sufficient. Nothing in the entire world could make me endure it a second time.”
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0002 }

“I think you’d have taken part in the run yourself had you been present,” Rupert grumbled.
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0003 }

“Coming from an elderly female wrapped in a piece of cotton fabric,” taunted Tobias. “Ho, ho, ho!”
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0004 }

“It failed to resemble an old woman in the least,” Grace exclaimed. “It was merely a huge, large, white object wriggling around in the grass precisely how Mary Stubbs stated Henry Warren did. Laughing is all well and good for you, Tobias Ashdown, but your laughter would have turned to distress had you been present. And in what manner will we receive punishment? Though I consider it unfair, inform us of what we must perform, Judge Ashdown!”
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0005 }

“In my opinion,” Tobias stated with a scowl, “Rupert holds the greatest responsibility. From what I gather, he was the first to run away. Furthermore, being a boy, he ought to have held his position so as to safeguard you girls, regardless of the peril. Isn’t that right, Rupert?”
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0006 }

“I guess so,” muttered Rupert with a look of shame.
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0007 }

“All right. Here is what your punishment will be. You will sit by yourself on the tombstone of Mr. Hezekiah Pollock in the cemetery tonight, up to twelve o’clock.”
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0008 }

Rupert trembled slightly. The old Bailey garden was located not particularly far from the cemetery. Although it promised to be a difficult test, Rupert eagerly desired to clear his dishonor and demonstrate that he was not, in fact, a faint-hearted person.
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0009 }

“Very well,” he replied with resolve. “However, in what way will I recognize the moment it reaches twelve?”
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0010 }

“You will hear the clock chime because the study windows are unclosed. And see to it that you do not move from that graveyard before the final chime ends. Regarding you girls, you must abstain from jam at supper for seven days.”
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0011 }

Grace and Ida wore somewhat bewildered expressions. They tended to believe that Rupert's relatively brief, albeit intense, suffering was a less severe penalty than this extended, lingering trial. An entire seven days of damp bread lacking the redeeming presence of jam! Nevertheless, no evading of duties was allowed within the club. The girls embraced their fate with whatever stoicism they were able to muster.
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0012 }

When nine o'clock arrived that evening, every one of them retired to bed, with the exception of Rupert, who was at that moment already maintaining his watch upon the tombstone. Ida crept inside so that she could wish him a good night. The deep sympathy she felt caused her gentle heart to ache.
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0013 }

“Oh, Rupert, are you very frightened?” she murmured.
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0014 }

“By no means,” Rupert stated lightheartedly.
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0015 }

“Not a wink of sleep will I get until twelve has passed,” Ida stated. “Should you become lonely, simply gaze toward our window and keep in mind that I am in there, awake, and contemplating you. Will that not offer a bit of companionship?”
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0016 }

“Do not fret over my well-being, for I shall be fine,” Rupert remarked.
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0017 }

Yet regardless of his brave statement, Rupert felt quite isolated once the manse’s lights were extinguished. It had been his hope to find his father in the study, where he frequently spent his time. In that case, loneliness would not have touched him. However, Mr. Ashdown had been called away that evening to the harbour mouth's fishing village to visit a man who was dying. His return was unlikely to occur before midnight had passed. Rupert had to endure his fate by himself.
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0018 }

A man from the Glen walked by, holding a lantern in his hand. The bizarre shadows produced by the illumination of the lantern rushed wildly across the cemetery, resembling a dance of witches or demons. Afterwards, those passed by, and shade returned once more. Individually, the Glen’s lights ceased to shine. The night was exceedingly dark, featuring a sky full of clouds, alongside an unpleasantly cold east wind that felt chilly regardless of what the calendar indicated. Distant on the horizon lay the faint, muted glow belonging to the Port Marlow lights. Within the ancient fir-trees, the wind moaned and breathed softly. Through the darkness, the lofty monument of Mr. Hector Twiss shone pale. Beside it, the willow flung out lengthy, twisting branches like a ghost. Now and then, the spinning of its limbs created the illusion that the monument was likewise in motion.
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0019 }

Rupert drawn his legs beneath himself as he curled up on top of the tombstone. Letting them dangle over the side of the stone was not particularly agreeable. Imagine—just imagine—if skeletal hands were to extend upward from Mr. Pollock’s underlying grave and grab him around his ankles. When they had all been gathered in that spot on a past occasion, Mary Stubbs had offered that bright thought. The idea came back to torment Rupert in this moment. He gave no credit to such notions; he did not even truly credit the ghost of Henry Warren. Regarding Mr. Pollock, sixty years had passed since his death, making it improbable that he minded who perched on his tombstone at present. Nevertheless, an immense strangeness and dread accompany being conscious while everyone else in the world sleeps. In those moments, you stand by yourself, possessing merely your own weak personality to match against the vast principalities and powers of darkness. Rupert was merely ten, surrounded on every side by the deceased—and he wished, oh, how he wished the clock would chime twelve. Was it ever going to chime twelve? Aunt Martha had certainly neglected to wind it.
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0020 }

And subsequently the hour of eleven rang out—merely eleven! An additional hour had to be spent by him in that dreary location. If merely a handful of welcoming stars could be spotted! The gloom possessed such density that his face appeared to be pushed by it. An impression of quiet, roving footsteps echoed throughout the cemetery. Rupert shuddered, caused in part by tingling dread and in part by actual chilliness.
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0021 }

A cold, soaking drizzle then started to fall. The thin cotton blouse and shirt worn by Rupert were quickly soaked. A deep cold reached his bones. His physical misery caused him to forget his psychological fears. Nevertheless, he was bound to remain in that spot until twelve, as he was enforcing his own punishment and bound by his honor. Although rain had not been mentioned, that altered nothing. As the study clock at last chimed twelve, a soaking wet small form climbed stiffly off the tombstone of Mr. Pollock, walked into the manse, and went up to bed. The teeth in Rupert’s mouth were knocking together. It seemed to him that he would be cold forever.
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0022 }

By the time morning arrived, he had become warm enough. Tobias cast a single alarmed glance at his flushed face and subsequently hurried to summon his father. Mr. Ashdown arrived in haste, his personal countenance pale as ivory from the faintness caused by his night-long watch beside a deathbed. Daylight had already broken when he finally reached home. With great anxiety, he leaned down over his young boy.
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0023 }

“Are you ill, Rupert?” he asked.
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0024 }

“That—gravestone—right here,” Rupert said, “it’s—shifting—around—it’s advancing—toward—me—hold it—back—I beg you.”
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0025 }

Mr. Ashdown hurried over to the phone. Dr. Carrow reached the manse within ten minutes. A telegram requesting a trained nurse was dispatched to town thirty minutes afterward, and the entire Glen learned that Rupert Ashdown had fallen gravely sick with pneumonia, with Dr. Carrow having been observed shaking his head.
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0026 }

More than a single time during the two weeks that came next, Hugh moved his head side to side. Double pneumonia struck Rupert. Mr. Ashdown walked back and forth across his study floor during a particular night, while Grace and Ida drew close together weeping in their bedroom, and Tobias, frantic with guilt, would not move away from the hall floor just beyond Rupert’s door. Neither Dr. Carrow nor the nurse departed from the bedside. Until the crimson sunrise, they bravely battled death, and they achieved the win. Rupert gained strength and safely survived the critical moment. Throughout the expectant Glen, the update was telephoned, and folk discovered the true depth of affection they held for their minister and his children.
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0027 }

“Since learning about the child’s illness, a single good night of sleep has eluded me,” Miss Winifred said to Nell, “and the weeping of Mary Stubbs has continued until her peculiar eyes resembled singed openings in a blanket. Did Rupert really contract pneumonia because he wandered into the graveyard on that rain-soaked night to satisfy a dare?”
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0028 }

“No. His reason for remaining in that place was self-punishment due to his lack of courage regarding the Warren ghost incident. Apparently, they belong to a club dedicated to self-improvement, where members inflict penalties on themselves for misdeeds. The whole story was relayed by Tobias to Mr. Ashdown.”
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0029 }

“The poor little souls,” Miss Winifred said.
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0030 }

Rupert recovered quickly, because the members of the church brought a sufficient amount of nutritious items to the manse to stock a hospital. Lionel Fairlie came by in his vehicle each night carrying twelve newly laid eggs alongside a pot of Jersey cream. On occasion, he remained for sixty minutes to shout debates concerning predestination alongside Mr. Ashdown inside the study; more frequently, he continued driving up toward the hill that had a view over the Glen.
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0031 }

A unique celebration was held in his celebration upon Rupert’s return to Fern Hollow, where the doctor joined the group to assist with the pyrotechnics. Although Mary Stubbs also attended, she refrained from sharing ghost tales, having received a lecture on the matter from Miss Winifred that Mary was unlikely to soon forget.
{: #nw-v05-c31-p0032 }
